name: Alpha-MSH

card.summary: The body's own tanning peptide: it switches on the MC1 receptor on pigment cells to make melanin, and its synthetic analogues are what the tanning-peptide scene is built around.
card.note: Native hormone; the synthetic analogues sold as tanning peptides are not approved for tanning.

quick.overview:
Alpha-MSH is a 13-amino-acid hormone made in the body from the precursor POMC. Its best-known job is stimulating melanin production in skin and hair through the MC1 receptor, which sets skin and hair colour.

It matters for appearance because synthetic versions of it, such as afamelanotide and melanotan II, are the compounds behind tanning-peptide use. Wikipedia notes that these analogues are far more potent than the natural hormone, with different selectivity.
quick.how: Alpha-MSH itself is not a consumer product. People interested in tanning typically discuss its synthetic analogues, which are injected, and which have effects beyond skin colour because the same family of receptors also influences appetite and sexual function.
quick.risks: Because alpha-MSH acts on several melanocortin receptors, MC3 and MC4 affect appetite, metabolism and sexual behaviour. Analogues of it are approved for specific medical uses only: afamelanotide for erythropoietic protoporphyria photosensitivity and bremelanotide for hypoactive sexual desire disorder in premenopausal women.

lead: Alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH) is a peptide hormone and neuropeptide of the melanocortin family. Wikipedia describes it as a 13-amino-acid peptide cleaved from ACTH(1-13), itself derived from the precursor proopiomelanocortin (POMC), and as the most important of the melanocyte-stimulating hormones for driving melanin production [1].

Its appearance role is pigmentation. By activating the MC1 receptor on melanocytes it shifts the cells from making yellow-red pheomelanin to brown-black eumelanin, which sets skin and hair colour and underlies tanning [1][9]. Natural variants of the MC1 receptor that work less well are common in people with red hair and light skin [9].

Most appearance interest centres on synthetic analogues rather than the hormone itself. Afamelanotide (melanotan I) was developed at the University of Arizona as a sunless-tanning candidate and is now approved, as the Scenesse implant, for erythropoietic protoporphyria; melanotan II and its offshoot bremelanotide followed [7][8][10]. Unregulated melanotan products sold for tanning are discussed in forums such as T Nation, and several health agencies have issued warnings about them since 2007 [3][4][8].
Because the same family of receptors acts in the brain, α-MSH and its analogues also influence appetite, energy balance and sexual behaviour through MC3 and MC4 receptors [1][10].

angle.text: Alpha-MSH is the natural signal for pigment production. Its synthetic analogues are used in tanning-peptide communities to darken skin without relying only on sun exposure.

infobox: 13 amino acids, N-acetylated and C-amidated; C77H109N21O19S, about 1,665 g/mol [1]
MC1, MC3, MC4, MC5 (not MC2, which responds only to ACTH) [1]
Ki about 0.23 nM at MC1, versus about 31.5 nM at MC3 and 900 nM at MC4 [1]
Melanin production in skin and hair through MC1 [1][9]
Afamelanotide for EPP photosensitivity (EU 2015, US 2019); bremelanotide for HSDD in premenopausal women (US 2019) [7][2][10]

paras: POMC is a precursor polypeptide cut by prohormone convertases into several peptides: ACTH, which regulates glucocorticoid release from the adrenal cortex, α-MSH, which acts on appetite, sexual behaviour and melanin in skin, and the opioid peptide β-endorphin [11]. The gene is expressed in the anterior and intermediate pituitary, in neurons of the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus and some other brain regions, and in skin melanocytes; human keratinocytes and melanocytes are also described as secreting POMC products that stimulate melanogenesis [11]. α-MSH is produced by proteolytic cleavage of ACTH(1-13) [1].

α-MSH is a non-selective full agonist at the melanocortin receptors MC1, MC3, MC4 and MC5 but not MC2, which responds only to ACTH. Reported binding constants are about 0.23 nM for MC1, 31.5 nM for MC3, 900 nM for MC4 and about 7,160 nM for MC5, which makes MC1, the pigment receptor, its highest-affinity target [1].

MC1 is a G protein-coupled receptor on melanocytes that couples to Gs and raises cAMP. Activation by α-MSH shifts melanocytes from default pheomelanin to eumelanin, and the receptor's natural antagonist agouti signalling peptide pushes cells back toward pheomelanin [9]. MC1 signalling also stimulates antioxidant and DNA-repair pathways in the UV response [9].

This is the biology behind sunless-tanning peptides: analogues that activate MC1 more strongly and for longer than the native hormone darken skin and hair pigment. Wikipedia reports that the analogues are much more potent than α-MSH, with improved pharmacokinetics and different receptor selectivity [1]. A T Nation poster quotes a research statement that α-MSH and ACTH increase proliferation and melanogenesis of cultured human melanocytes [3].

Loss-of-function MC1 variants are common among people with red hair; Asp294His, Arg151Cys and Arg160Trp are the best known, and many redheads carry more than one [9]. POMC deficiency in humans is associated with early-onset obesity, adrenal insufficiency and red hair pigmentation [11]. Some MC1 variants are also risk factors for basal and squamous cell skin cancer independent of pigmentation, and MC1 is highly expressed in melanomas [9].

A 2024 review of alopecia areata and vitiligo notes that α-MSH is one of the immunomodulatory factors suppressed when immune privilege collapses in hair follicles [6]. A 2023 review of GLP-1 lists α-MSH among peptides with receptor-mediated anti-inflammatory properties [12].

The University of Arizona developed early α-MSH analogues in the 1980s, including melanotan I, first studied as a sunless-tanning agent. Competitive Technologies licensed it to the Australian start-up Epitan, which became Clinuvel in 2006, and a slow-release implant was developed because early versions needed about ten injections a day [7].

Afamelanotide, sold as Scenesse, is given as a subcutaneous implant. Italy approved it in May 2010, the European Medicines Agency in January 2015, and the US FDA in October 2019 to increase pain-free light exposure in adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria, a rare genetic sun sensitivity [7]. Clinuvel also sponsored studies from 2007 to 2011 in vitiligo, polymorphous light eruption, solar urticaria and acne, and later trials covered vitiligo and other conditions [7]. The most common side effects are nausea, headache and implant-site reactions, and because it can darken existing skin lesions, full-body skin checks every six months are often recommended [7].

subs.h: Melanotan II and the tanning-peptide scene
paras: Melanotan II was synthesised at the same university. Early 1960s work had found that α-MSH caused sexual arousal in rats, and one researcher who injected twice his intended dose reported a long erection with nausea and vomiting [8]. Competitive Technologies licensed melanotan II to Palatin Technologies for sexual dysfunction; Palatin stopped development in 2000 and pursued bremelanotide, and a lawsuit settled in 2008 returned the rights to Competitive Technologies [8].

Products sold online, in gyms and in beauty salons as melanotan variants are used for tanning and are not legally sold for human use in any jurisdiction, according to Wikipedia [8]. A 2010 review in the British Journal of Dermatology asked whether melanotropic peptides were more than 'Barbie drugs' and 'sun-tan jabs' [8]. Media coverage from 2009 included the BBC reporting that tan-jab warnings were ignored and CBS coverage of 'tanorexia' [8].

Palatin Technologies developed bremelanotide after melanotan II. An intranasal form was halted by the FDA in 2007 over blood-pressure increases, and the injectable form (Vyleesi) was approved in June 2019 for generalised hypoactive sexual desire disorder in premenopausal women [10][2]. It acts mainly at MC3 and MC4 receptors [10]. Reported side effects include nausea in about 40 percent of trial participants, flushing, injection-site reactions and headache, a temporary rise in blood pressure, and darkening of the gums, face and breasts that may not resolve after stopping [10]. A 2003 report described PT-141 producing dose-dependent erectile activity in normal men and men with erectile dysfunction [5].

sections.h: Reported adverse effects of tanning analogues
paras: Reported effects of melanotan products include reversible darkening of moles and freckles, flushing, nausea, vomiting, yawning, appetite loss and erections in men [8]. Whether they raise melanoma risk is unclear: a 2013 review found no conclusive evidence of causation, a 2021 review attributed higher melanoma rates among users to greater UV exposure, and a 2020 in vivo study reported suppressed melanoma progression [8].

Health agencies have warned against melanotan products since 2007, including the Norwegian Medicines Agency (December 2007), the Danish Medicines Agency and UK MHRA (2008), and the FDA, which issued a warning letter to a US supplier on 29 January 2009 [8].

On T Nation, melanotan I and II are discussed in a 2008 sticky that claims the peptides increase pigmentation without UV, though UV speeds tanning, with strongest tanning on the face, arms, abdomen and genitals; the author calls melanotan I the better of the two with less pronounced effects, while noting melanotan II is cheaper and more commonly chosen [4]. Other posters in a 2008 thread report anecdotes: a very dark tan with little UV, existing moles becoming darker and more prominent, and one poster's wife who tanned quickly and darkened further [3]. Another poster in the sticky thread disputed the post's accuracy and asked for its removal [4]. These accounts are anecdotal and are not clinical data.

No studies found of native α-MSH as a tanning agent. Human work covers analogues: afamelanotide for photoprotection and erythropoietic protoporphyria and trials in other light-sensitive conditions [7], bremelanotide's approval for hypoactive sexual desire disorder [2][10], and an early trial of PT-141 in men [5]. Research on α-MSH itself in rodents includes protection against ischaemia and reperfusion injury in a rat retinal model [1].

lore.intro: On T Nation, α-MSH comes up in discussion of melanotan I and II, with posters sharing peptide structures, research on melanocyte stimulation, tanning anecdotes and warnings about moles [3][4].

claims.claim: α-MSH analogues stimulate melanocytes to make more melanin and darken skin
claims.believers: Forum members cite studies that α-MSH and ACTH increase melanocyte proliferation and melanogenesis and use this to explain the tan from melanotan [3].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that MC1 activation by α-MSH drives pigmentation and that afamelanotide has been approved for a photosensitivity disorder [1][7].

claims.claim: Melanotan gives a dark tan with little sun
claims.believers: A 2008 sticky says the peptides increase pigmentation without UV exposure, though sun greatly speeds the effect, and posters describe users who become very dusky [4][3].
claims.experts: Afamelanotide's trials focused on photoprotection in EPP rather than cosmetic tanning, and unregulated melanotan products are not approved for tanning [7][8].

claims.claim: Melanotan I is milder than melanotan II
claims.believers: A T Nation author calls melanotan I the better of the two, with less pronounced side effects but higher cost and slower action [4].
claims.experts: No published comparison of the two for tanning is available; Wikipedia lists nausea, flushing and appetite loss for melanotan II products [8].

claims.claim: Melanotan darkens existing moles and may add new ones
claims.believers: Posters say it 'makes existing ones a lot darker and more prominent' and repeat hearsay of outbreaks of new moles [3].
claims.experts: Reversible darkening of moles and freckles is listed among reported effects; the link to melanoma is unclear, with reviews pointing to UV exposure as a confounder [8].

claims.claim: Melanotan II also boosts libido and suppresses appetite
claims.believers: The sticky lists increased libido and prolonged arousal for melanotan II and appetite suppression for both [4].
claims.experts: The same receptor family regulates appetite and sexual behaviour through MC3 and MC4, and bremelanotide is approved for low desire in premenopausal women [1][10].

claims.claim: Unregulated melanotan products are safe enough for home use
claims.believers: Some posters describe the side effects as mainly minor nausea, appetite suppression and flushing [4].
claims.experts: Health agencies have warned against the products since 2007 and Wikipedia states they are not legal for human use in any jurisdiction [8].
